PSI U PERSONALITY OF THE MONTH
S. Spencer Scott, Phi '14
By James M. Reid, Zeta '24
UNLIKE
most successful book publish
ers, S. Spencer Scott (Phi '14, Uni
versity of Michigan) is not a
disappointed
author. Rather, he is a
hterary business
man and salesman. If he can
publish a
book which brings forth superlatives from
the hterary doctors and also sell a
couple
of carloads, all his powers, as one author
said, are
functioning harmoniously.
Spencer is today the second in com
mand at Harcourt, Brace and Company.
He is Vice President and General Man
ager. In his twenty-seven
years on the job
he has helped to build the company from
a
gleam in Alfred Harcourt's and Donald
Brace's eyes (1919) to the point where the
textbook department alone is today one of
the ten largest in the industry.
Daily, Spence arrives at the fifth floor
of 383 Madison Avenue (right across from
the Ritz) hot on the heels of the reception
ist who turns the key and opens the place
for business, well ahead of the 138 other
employees. For Spence, despite the fact
that he is number two man and third
largest stockholder, still looks upon him
self as an
employee. Unless he has an
author in tow, he habitually uses the em
ployees' entrance by the shipping room,
rather than parade through the hand
some, booklined reception, room. There is
no time-clock at Harcourt, Brace, but
inost of the staff is aware that the Vice
President gets there early�and stays until
the 5:45 for Scarsdale.
For many years Spence helped the
people at the mail desk open and distrib
ute the mail, but today he pitches at once
into his many-sided job. He is in direct
charge of trade sales (the two thousandodd book stores of the country are knowni
as the "trade"; hence the department which
publishes books of fiction, biography; and
such, and distributes them to the general
public through the book stores is knowTi
as the "trade department," as opposed to
the "text department*^. Spence vidll scarce
ly have warmed the seat of the chair in
his spacious ofiice (formerly Alfred Har
court's, who retired in 1942) more than a
few minutes before the head salesman is
at his elbow concerning a
problem of dis
counts or
hiring a new man. Or the manu
facturing man hurries in to bemoan scant
paper supplies and shortages of press time,
or to ask Spence to look into his crystal
ball and specify how many copies of a
fast-moving novel to print. The line which
forms outside of Spence's office is apt to
include people from the juvenile depart
ment, ti'ade publicity, shipping, office
management, or credit departments�all of
which are under his direct supei-vision.
The text department, which Spence
headed and developed over a
period of
more than twenty years, is still under his
supervision, but it moves
along today with
out making serious demands on his time.
A former president of the University of
Illinois once said that even a fair-sized
textbook department hke Harcourt, Brace's
carries educational weight equivalent to
that of a
good-sized university. Starting in
1920 in charge of the textbook depart
ment in place of Will Howe (it was Har
court, Brace and Howe originally), Spence
built a textbook list which now includes
over three hundred titles and a staff of
twenty salesmen.
Spence has never been merely an office
boss. Not a
year has gone by without his
having done some active selling. Until re
cently he made two visits a
year with a
bag of books in his hand to some
fifty
New York City high schools^ a dozen
junior high schools, the University of
Michigan, West Pomt, and Annapolis.
Even today, devoting most of his energies
to the trade rather than the text depart
ment, he calls regularly on certain New
York City book stores. It was he who
initiated and maintained the policy of al
ways recruiting his textbook editors from
the sales staff and never
directly from the

THE DIAMOND OF PSI UPSILON 3
schools or
by raids on other publishers.
The new
thing contributed by Spence
to textbook pubhshing is summed up in
his slogan, "Modem books for the schools."
Back in the early twenties, for almost aU
high school pupils in English classes, lit
erature was
something written by dead
men. With missionary zeal Spence pub
hshed for both high schools and colleges
a whole string of modern literature books
to
give visible proof to students that lit
erature is not a dead thing, but a
living,
going concern.
Christopher Morley's
Modern Essays was the first coUection of
strictly contemporary essays for schools
and colleges. Untermeyer's Modern Poetry,
Cohen's One Act Plays by Modern
Authors, Schweikert's Short Stories, Chamberlaia's Essays Old and New, Hyde's
Modern Biography-all of these, still in
print and actively selling twenty to
hventy-five years later, provided welcome
alternatives to the time-worn "classics"�
Ivanhoe, Silas Marner, Idylls of the King,
and so on ad boredom. It was not always
easy to get contemporary authors to give
permission for their works to be reprinted,
but Spence persistently convinced them
that representation in a textbook which
would be not
only read but also studied by
hundreds of thousands of young people
was the best form of contemporary im
mortality.
In other departments of the curriculum,
Spence also built a durable list. He says
it's more fun to be a
pioneer and pubhsh
a
daring new kind of book than it is to do
the safe and repetitious book. J. Russell
Smith's North America is a
good example.
When it was
published in 1924 there were
only twelve courses in the geography of
North America in the colleges of the coun
try. Within two years North Arrierica had
125 adoptions�obviously over a hundred
colleges were stimulated to put in a new
course by the appearance of a first good
book. Kroeber's Anthropology (1923) set
some kind of a
publishing record when,
in 1946, it led its field in sales and had its
largest sales total without revision in
twenty-three years. Schevill's A History of
Europe (1923), revised approximately
every five years, is still the leading onevolume text in European history for col
leges. Pairington's Main Currents in Amer
ican Thought, today regarded as one of
our intellectual classics, was discovered by
Spence and first contracted for as a text
book, though when pubhshed it was
brought out in the trade edition.
Although Spence has many outside in
terests, he has often been a
minority. For
example, he is a Democrat in rock-ribbed,
Republican Scarsdale. A socialist as a
young man, he voted four times for FDR.
He has the moral stamina and tough de
termination demanded of a
minority fight
er. He has had the usual executive's ulcer,
precipitateid more, some of his associates
say, by the daily strain of laying off
cigarettes until after lunph than by the
erosion of manifold responsibilities in the
dizzying world of today. He is no
bigger,
210 pounds on the hoof, than when he
played tackle on the Michigan varsity in
1913. And he is as blonde and imweathered and healthy looking as ever.
But despite this ama of youth and health
he seems to get more than his share of
minor miseries, such as
scraping off a
dozen square inches of hide by slipping
off the boardwalk at Pouit o'Woods, teeth
which are even and pretty but as trouble
some as
George VVashington's, enough
spills on horseback that the board of di
rectors at HB Co. threatened to serve him
with an
injimction.
In World War I, Spence had a
highly
educational post as
sergeant in the Medi
cal Corps in charge of botthng whiskey for
overseas
shipment. He became sophisti
cated in the ways of whiskey and this has
stood him in good stead through Prohibi
tion, two booms, and one
depression. For
nearly twenty years after World War I,
Spence was a familiar figure in white on
the end of a whistle, officiating football
games from Dartmouth to Upsala. He mar
ried Edna Minsinger of Portland, Oregon,
in 1919 and has two children�Carolyn
(Smith '42) who saw overseas service in
the Red Cross during the war," and S.
Spencer, Jr., a
flyer in the Air Corps and
currently a senior at Princeton.

Albert W. Tolman, Jr.
ALBERT
W. TOLMAN, JR., Kappa
i '25, was bom in Portland, Maine, on
Jime 8, 1904, and is a son of Albert W.
Tolman, Kappa '88 and a brother of Ed
ward M. Tolman, Kappa '27.
He was educated at Portland High
School, Bowdoin College (A.B. cum laude
'25), and New York University (M.B.A. '27
and LL.B. '36), and is presently a GI stuAlbert W. Tolman, Jr., Kappa '25
dent in the graduate division of New York
University's School of Law. Tolman is a
certffied public accountant and a member
of the New York and District of Colimibia
Bars. At Bowdoin he played on the hockey
and tennis teams and, for a
year, served
as managing editor of the college paper.
After graduation from Bowdoin he con
tinued his association with the fraternity
through membership in the Psi Upsilon
Club of New York and for a number of
years was treasurer of that organization.
Brother Tolman has been employed in
public accounting or investment banking
in New York City since 1925, except for
about seven
years, three and a half of
which he was in the Army of the United
States. After serving in Italy during 1944
as statistician and economist for the Food
subcommission of the Allied Control Com
mission, he returned to the United States
and, until his release from the Array in
1946, was in charge of the renegotiation
of war contracts for the Quartermaster
Corps. Lt. Col. Tolman was awarded the
Bronze Star for service in Italy and the
Legion of Merit for his work in contract
renegotiation.
Since his return to civiHan life, he has
been engaged in .the practice of pubhc ac
counting with the New York office of the
firm of Peat, Marwick, Mitchell & Co.
Al and his family consisting of Mrs.
Tolman and their three children, Charles,
Mary, and Deborah, live in Mamaroneck,
New York, and enjoy spending their vaca
tions in Maine.
Russell S. Callow, Theta Theta '16
It was
fitting that Rusty Callow, as he
is affectionately knowTi to thousands of
undergraduates and alumni, should have
been elected to the Executive Council at
the first Convention of 'the Fratemity to
be held with the Theta Theta Chapter. A
Charter member of that Chapter and its
first presiding officer, he had proposed the
toast to "The Theta Theta" at the installa
tion banquet on
June 10, 1916, just over
thirty-one years before.
Brother Callow has been a member of
the Board of Governors of the Alumni As
sociation of Psi Upsilon for the past thir
teen years. He is a lffe member of the As
sociation.
He matriculated at the University of
Washington in 1911, after graduating from
Olympia High School two years previously,
and teaching elementary school in the in
terim. In his sophomore year he was on
the varsity football squad and on the var
sity eight that rowed 'at Poughkeepsie, and
was elected crew
captain a
year later, after
his second regatta on the Hudson. Among
his non-athletic honors were election as

president of the Associated Students, presi
dency of both the senior and jimior hon
orary societies, membership in Phi Delta
-Kappa, honorary educational fratemity,
and Sigma Upsilon, college literary fra
ternity. He became affiliated with the local
sociely. Phi Kappa, organized in 1909,
whose primary purpose was to achieve a
charter of Psi Upsilon. Phi Kappa pre
sented its first petition to the 1911 Con
vention and continued its efforts until the
Convention of 1915, held with the Epsilon
Chapter, approved its petition.
After his graduation in 1916 until 1922,
Brother Callow was
employed in teaching
in the history department of the University
of Washington and as
superintendent of
his family lumber company. In 1922 the
University callpd him back as crew coach.
His varsity crews were victorious at
Pough
keepsie in 1923, 1924 and 1926, finishing
second in 1925 and 1927.
In 1927, Brother CaUow became crew
coach at the University of Pennsylvania,
and m 1929 the varsity eight defeated
Navy and Harvard and finished third to
Columbia and Washington in the Pough
keepsie regatta. In 1935 a
Pennsylvania
crew won the Blackwell, Adams and Childs
Cup regattas.
World War II intermpted Rusty's
coaching career in October, 1942, when
he obtained leave of absence from Penn
sylvania to accept a War job in Seattle,
where he became personnel director of the
Webster-Brinkley Company, makers of
engines for L.C.I, and L.S.T. boats and
other naval equipment. When he left
Webster-Brinkley to return to Pennsyl
vania, the huge industrial plant was closed
for half an hour and at a
public ceremony
Brother Callow was
presented with a
painting of himself with a bronze plaque
bearing this inscription:
"Russell S. 'Rusty' Callow
Personnel Director 1942-1945
In Appreciation For Selfless Service
A Distinguished Contribution to War
Production
From the Employees and
Management of Webster-Brinkley
Co., Seattle, Washington."
Mrs. Callow, whom Brother Callow met
in his undergraduate days, when she was
secretary of the Associated Students at
Washington University duriog his presi
dency of that organization, has been active
in the affairs of her coUege sorority.

ury. Before coining to the Treasury post he

grad
uate of Columbia University, has held an

ner of the Newcomb Medal at the Franklin

Dr. Goodrich C. Schauffler,
Delta Delta 'IB
Brother Schauffler has given up a
large
Portland, Oregon, practice to accept a
UNRRA assignment to instruct ia his
specialty, gynecology and obstetrics, in
China.
According to an article pubhshed in the
May 4 issue of The Sunday Oregonian,
"From his observations of tiie daily hfe
in China, Dr. Schauffler is of the opinion
that it is perhaps more
important for
United States citizens to understand the
Chinese people and to sympathize with
their problems than to send them money
or
goods. 'No amount of money or of
supplies can
bridge the gulf between the
western and the oriental psychologies,'
the doctor maintained. To illustrate his
meaning, he cited the reluctance of United
States hospitals to give doctors from China
appointments as residents or interns. Their
first obhgations are to their own men, they
explain. Dr. Schauffler, who has seen the
desperate need) feels that each of these
hospitals could do China an immeasurable
amount of good by somehow making room
for one or two of her doctors. American
plenty makes it far too easy to continue
in a
superficial, actually a
provincial, at
titude toward the great suffering nations
of the Orient,' the Portland physician con
cluded. 'Only through complete under
standing can the spiritual and the intellec
tual gap be closed in the interest of an
eventual union of nations.'
"
Alexis Caswell, Sigma '90

grandson of
Dr. Alexis Caswell, one-time Brown Uni
versity president, has announced his re
tirement from business and will enjoy the

served as
manager and secretary of the
Manufacturers' Association of Minneapolis
since 1919 and as consultant to the manu

merce. He was
secretary-treasurer for years
of nine organizations: American Society
for Metals, Foreman's club. National As
sociation of Cost Accoimtants, Northwest

Society, Insurance Buyers Association of
Minnesota, American Foundrymen's as
sociation and the Twin Cities Plastics as
